chapter: Joining Goodman and views on arranging
title: Fritz Reiner and his conducting
summary: Anecdotes of Reiner's courtesy and hypnotic small beat.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: That was an experience, to work under Reiner.
What was his attitude towards the whole project?
Very, very, very nice. Everything I heard about him did not come to pass.
He had a mambo section in there; I guess the composer had written things and Mousey--

At one point, Mousey raises his hand and the whole works stops and he said, Dr. Reiner, it doesn't go like that, and there was a shocked silence, because they just wouldn't do that. I guess he felt that well, here are these guests and I'll treat them like guests. So he said, how do you think they should go and Mousey showed him and he said okay, you do it that way.

He had Sonny Russo come out and audition because he liked so much the way he played, and Sonny said, unfortunately I can't because you don't know the literature. So Sonny came back and tried to learn the literature, but it didn't go. I guess he died shortly after that anyway.
I remember before we went on that night, he took Bill and I into his little cubicle--he had a little cubicle backstage and a bottle of bourbon and said, would you like a little nip. He said I

always take one before I go on. So we all had a little nip, and he said the secret to all this is getting the good men. That's what it means to be a good conductor, to get the good players. It was something we all knew, but I didn't expect it to come from him.

Then we got some experience, because I think he conducted through hypnosis. His motions of about an inch by a half inch and you would look very close and it was those burning eyes that seemed to have control over everything. (Inaudible)
He really had control and a conductor is supposed to.
There's a story of one percussionist who at one point got out a spy glass and he stopped the orchestra and said, what are you doing. He said I'm trying to find your beat. I guess he lost his job too.
I saw Stokowski conduct a few years before he died, that's

when he had the American Symphony, in the early seventies, and by that time he was close to ninety and his conducting was the same way. There was a definite beat but it was very small strokes, and you really had to watch him closely, but it was still there. There was no question about it. There was no question that he was fully in control of that orchestra.
It's a hidden authority; it's a weird thing.
